    What the network learned

    Card checks

    How it plays. Every one of the 449 different cards in these decks has its rules text handled: a general parser covers the common patterns, and the rest have their own scripts. That includes the combos: Sanguine Bond, Vito, Dina or Enduring Tenacity with Exquisite Blood or Bloodthirsty Conqueror; Basalt Monolith with Rings of Brighthearth into Staff of Domination, Aetherflux Reservoir or Walking Ballista; Karn with Mycosynth Lattice; and death-trigger drains with sacrifice outlets. Effects that multiply each other stack the way they should: token and counter doublers, Fiery Emancipation and Gisela, Terror of the Peaks with Dragon tokens, extra combats with Kaalia. Each player is a heuristic AI steered by a small neural network trained on thousands of self-play games (see "What the network learned"). It sees the board, plays to win and holds up counterspells and protection. On engine and combo turns it looks ahead: it tries its best few plays on a copy of the game, plays out the rest of the turn, and keeps the line that ends best. When choosing whom to attack it weighs who is most likely to win, the way a real pod gangs up on the leader. It still won't find every line a strong human would. Click any card to read it. Space plays and pauses, and the arrow keys step through the game. Card data comes from the open-source Forge project. Card art is generic, picked by creature or card type, using icons by the artists at game-icons.net (CC BY 3.0). Decks: Edgar (100 cards), Kaalia (100 cards), Beledros (100 cards), Atraxa (100 cards), Osgir (100 cards), Myrkul (100 cards), Muldrotha (100 cards).
